title: From Result to Therapy: MSSA Penicillinase, C. difficile, Giardia and Inpatient Influenza
summary: Learn what four common microbiology results mean for the next step: penicillinase-positive MSSA, C. difficile infection drug choice, first-line Giardia therapy, and antivirals plus precautions for a hospitalized influenza positive.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 66 Hits 23, 27, 29 and 31. Checked against Takayama 2018, Coombs 2022, Corsini Campioli 2021, Brahma 2019 and Andrade-Figueiredo 2016 (S. aureus; Andrade-Figueiredo abstract only), Bainum 2023, Gu 2022 and Brown 2013 (C. difficile; Brown abstract only), Lalle 2018 and Pasupuleti 2014 (Giardia), the IDSA 2018 influenza guideline (Uyeki 2019; read via a page-fetch tool) and the CDC influenza infection-control page (page-fetch tool). Nuance: Hit 27 lists oral vancomycin first with fidaxomicin in brackets; the 2021 IDSA/SHEA focused update (as summarised by Bainum 2023) prefers fidaxomicin over vancomycin. Hit 23: rare oxacillin-susceptible mecA-positive strains (OS-MRSA) are reported. Not taught: drug doses, recurrent or fulminant CDI, PSSA penicillin therapy, influenza chemoprophylaxis.

objectives: Explain why a beta-lactamase-positive, oxacillin-susceptible S. aureus is MSSA and which drugs remain usable.
Name the preferred and endorsed drugs for C. difficile infection and the antibiotic class most linked to it.
State first-line Giardia therapy and the immediate actions for a positive influenza molecular test in a hospitalized patient.

scenes.title: Four results, four next moves
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four microbiology results are released on one ward round — (1) blood isolate of Staphylococcus aureus, oxacillin susceptible, beta-lactamase (penicillinase) positive; (2) stool positive for toxigenic Clostridioides difficile in a patient on clindamycin; (3) stool ova-and-parasite exam positive for Giardia; (4) inpatient with acute respiratory illness, influenza molecular assay positive, ill for 5 days. Question token: “What does each result change?”

cues.text: Four results land on one ward round: a Staphylococcus aureus blood isolate that is oxacillin susceptible but beta-lactamase positive, and a stool positive for toxin-producing C. difficile.
Then a stool positive for Giardia, and an inpatient, sick for five days, whose influenza molecular test is positive.
Each result should trigger a specific next move. What are they?

scenes.title: Penicillinase is not methicillin resistance
scenes.altText: Schematic: two separate resistance mechanisms in Staphylococcus aureus. Card 1: penicillinase (beta-lactamase, gene blaZ) inactivates penicillin G by hydrolysing its beta-lactam ring. Card 2: methicillin resistance comes from an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, encoded by mecA; an oxacillin-susceptible isolate is classified as methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) on susceptibility testing, although rare mecA-positive oxacillin-susceptible strains (OS-MRSA) are reported. Card 3: antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin) are the standard agents for MSSA, with cefazolin commonly used as an alternative. Card 4: penicillinase is inducible and not always expressed; nitrocefin tests can miss it, and CLSI/EUCAST pair nitrocefin with the penicillin zone-edge test.

cues.text: Staphylococcus aureus resists penicillin in two separate ways. Penicillinase, a beta-lactamase coded by the blaZ gene, breaks the beta-lactam ring of penicillin G.

Methicillin resistance is different: an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, coded by mecA. An oxacillin-susceptible isolate is classified as MSSA, even when it makes penicillinase, though rare mecA-positive strains test oxacillin susceptible.
So penicillin G is out, but the antistaphylococcal penicillins, nafcillin and oxacillin, are the standard drugs for MSSA, and cefazolin is commonly used as an alternative.
And a negative nitrocefin test does not prove penicillin susceptibility: penicillinase is inducible, so standards pair nitrocefin with the penicillin zone-edge test.

scenes.title: C. difficile and Giardia: which drug first
scenes.altText: Left: Clostridioides difficile infection. Guidelines endorse metronidazole, oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin. The 2017 IDSA/SHEA guideline removed metronidazole as a preferred option for mild disease; the 2021 focused update made fidaxomicin preferred over vancomycin; other guidelines still allow metronidazole for low-risk mild disease or when the other two are limited. Risk bar: in a meta-analysis of community-associated CDI, clindamycin carried the highest odds (OR about 17), fluoroquinolones about 5.5, tetracyclines no clear effect. Right: Giardia. Metronidazole is still considered the first-line antigiardial (cure about 80–95%) but has unpleasant side effects; tinidazole and related nitroimidazoles are single-day alternatives; an increase in nitroimidazole-refractory cases is reported in low-prevalence settings such as Europe, especially in travellers returning from Asia.

cues.text: C. difficile infection: guidelines endorse three drugs, metronidazole, oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin. IDSA and SHEA dropped metronidazole as preferred for mild disease in 2017, and their 2021 update prefers fidaxomicin over vancomycin.
Clindamycin is a cause, not a cure. In a meta-analysis of community-acquired cases, clindamycin carried the highest risk of all antibiotic classes, about seventeen-fold.

Giardia: metronidazole is still considered the first-line drug, curing about eighty to ninety-five percent, though side effects are common. Tinidazole and related drugs work in a single daily dose for one or a few days.
But nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis is reported to be rising in Europe, especially in travellers returning from Asia, so treatment failure needs follow-up.

scenes.title: A positive flu test in a hospitalized patient
scenes.altText: Influenza card (IDSA 2018): during influenza activity, test all patients hospitalized with acute respiratory illness on admission, using RT-PCR or another molecular assay; do not use rapid antigen tests in hospitalized patients unless molecular assays are unavailable; do not use viral culture for initial diagnosis. Treat hospitalized patients with influenza as soon as possible, regardless of illness duration before admission, with a single neuraminidase inhibitor; do not delay empiric treatment while results are pending. Precautions card (CDC): Droplet Precautions for 7 days after onset or until 24 hours after fever and respiratory symptoms resolve, whichever is longer; private room; staff wear a facemask. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Influenza in hospital: during flu activity, the 2018 IDSA guideline says to test admitted patients with acute respiratory illness using a molecular assay. Rapid antigen tests only if no molecular test is available, and viral culture is not for initial diagnosis.
A hospitalized patient with influenza gets a neuraminidase inhibitor as soon as possible, regardless of how many days they have been ill. Empiric treatment should not wait for results.
CDC adds Droplet Precautions: a private room and a facemask, for seven days after onset or until twenty-four hours after symptoms resolve, whichever is longer.

Hook answers: MSSA, so no penicillin G but nafcillin or oxacillin; C. difficile, so fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin, remembering clindamycin raises the risk; Giardia, metronidazole; influenza, antivirals now plus Droplet Precautions.

props.title: Test (IDSA 2018)
lines: Rapid antigen: only if no PCR

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Beta-lactamase positive S. aureus = MRSA” (✓ penicillinase defeats penicillin G only; oxacillin-susceptible = MSSA); “Metronidazole is the preferred drug for C. difficile” (✓ not preferred by IDSA/SHEA since 2017; fidaxomicin preferred, oral vancomycin endorsed); “Ill more than 2 days or test pending, so wait on antivirals” (✓ hospitalized patients are treated as soon as possible regardless of illness duration; do not wait for results).

cues.text: Trap one: a beta-lactamase positive Staphylococcus aureus is MRSA. No: penicillinase defeats penicillin G; oxacillin susceptible means MSSA.
Trap two: metronidazole is the preferred C. difficile drug. No: under IDSA and SHEA, fidaxomicin is preferred, and oral vancomycin is endorsed.
Trap three: a hospitalized flu patient ill for five days is too late for antivirals. No: treat as soon as possible, regardless of illness duration.

props.title: ✗ “Beta-lactamase + = MRSA.”
lines: ✓ Oxacillin S = MSSA; only penicillin G is lost

scenes.title: Scissors, swallow, nitro, now
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SCISSORS, SWALLOW, NITRO, NOW.” Scissors = penicillinase snips penicillin G, so an oxacillin-susceptible staph goes to nafcillin or oxacillin; Swallow = for C. difficile, vancomycin is given by mouth (oral vancomycin), with fidaxomicin preferred; Nitro = a nitroimidazole (metronidazole) for Giardia; Now = inpatient influenza gets antivirals now, without waiting. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: scissors, swallow, nitro, now. Scissors: penicillinase snips penicillin G, so MSSA gets nafcillin or oxacillin. Swallow: C. difficile gets oral vancomycin, or preferred fidaxomicin. Nitro: a nitroimidazole for Giardia. Now: inpatient flu gets antivirals now.

Where it breaks: metronidazole is also a nitroimidazole, still allowed for C. difficile in limited cases; fulminant C. difficile adds intravenous metronidazole; refractory Giardia is rising; and local guidelines decide final therapy.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Metronidazole: limited CDI role; IV in fulminant

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Beta-lactamase + / oxacillin S = MSSA → nafcillin or oxacillin, not penicillin G · CDI → fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin”, “Giardia → metronidazole · inpatient flu + → neuraminidase inhibitor now + Droplet Precautions”.

cues.text: Read each result as a therapy cue: a penicillinase-positive, oxacillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is MSSA treated with nafcillin or oxacillin rather than penicillin G, Clostridioides difficile infection gets fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin, Giardia gets metronidazole, and a hospitalized influenza positive gets antivirals now plus Droplet Precautions.

props.label: Beta-lactamase + / oxacillin S = MSSA → nafcillin · CDI → fidaxomicin
Giardia → metronidazole · inpatient flu + → antiviral now + droplet

explanation.what: Plain language: some lab results directly change treatment. A staph that makes penicillinase can still be killed by staph-specific penicillins if it is oxacillin susceptible; C. difficile is treated with fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin; Giardia is usually treated with metronidazole; and a hospital patient with flu should start antivirals at once and be placed on Droplet Precautions. Scientific terms: beta-lactamase (penicillinase, blaZ), PBP2a (mecA), MSSA, antistaphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin), cefazolin, fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin, 5-nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole), neuraminidase inhibitor, RT-PCR, rapid influenza diagnostic test (RIDT), Droplet Precautions.
explanation.why: Penicillinase hydrolyses the beta-lactam ring of penicillin G, while methicillin resistance needs PBP2a. CDI risk rises with antibiotics such as clindamycin; drug choice for CDI has shifted toward fidaxomicin. The IDSA guideline recommends antiviral treatment as soon as possible for hospitalized influenza, and CDC recommends Droplet Precautions for patients with suspected or confirmed influenza.
explanation.measure: S. aureus: oxacillin S + beta-lactamase + = MSSA on susceptibility testing (rare mecA-positive OS-MRSA exist), penicillin G inactive; nitrocefin can miss inducible penicillinase, so zone edge is also used. CDI: fidaxomicin preferred (2021), oral vancomycin endorsed, metronidazole not preferred by IDSA/SHEA since 2017 (other guidelines allow it for low-risk mild disease). Giardia: metronidazole first-line (cure about 80–95%), tinidazole single-day alternative. Influenza (IDSA 2018): molecular assay on admission; treat hospitalized patients ASAP regardless of illness duration; do not wait for results; CDC Droplet Precautions for 7 days or until 24 h after symptoms resolve, whichever is longer.
explanation.differs: Penicillinase (penicillin G only) vs PBP2a (methicillin/oxacillin resistance); fidaxomicin/oral vancomycin (treat CDI) vs clindamycin (precipitates CDI); molecular flu assay vs rapid antigen test vs viral culture.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: what a positive beta-lactamase means on an oxacillin-susceptible isolate, which drug treats or causes CDI, first-line Giardia therapy, and whether to start antivirals or wait in a hospitalized influenza patient.

comparisons.title: Penicillinase vs methicillin resistance
comparisons.distinguisher: Oxacillin result: susceptible = MSSA despite penicillinase.

comparisons.title: Treats CDI vs precipitates CDI
comparisons.distinguisher: Drugs that treat CDI vs antibiotic exposure that raises CDI risk.

mnemonic.text: SCISSORS, SWALLOW, NITRO, NOW: penicillinase snips penicillin G (MSSA gets nafcillin or oxacillin); C. difficile vancomycin is swallowed (oral vancomycin), with fidaxomicin preferred; a nitroimidazole (metronidazole) for Giardia; inpatient influenza gets antivirals now.
mnemonic.explanation: One cue word per result-to-therapy link.
mnemonic.limitation: Metronidazole is also a nitroimidazole that some guidelines still allow for low-risk CDI or when fidaxomicin and vancomycin are limited, and fulminant CDI regimens add intravenous metronidazole; nitroimidazole-refractory Giardia is reported to be rising; local guidelines and formularies decide final therapy.

analogyLimitations: Resistance mechanisms are drawn schematically as cards.
Drug preferences follow the guidelines cited; local policies differ.
takeaway: Read each result as a therapy cue: a penicillinase-positive, oxacillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is MSSA treated with nafcillin or oxacillin rather than penicillin G, Clostridioides difficile infection gets fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin, Giardia gets metronidazole, and a hospitalized influenza positive gets antivirals now plus Droplet Precautions.

questions.stem: A blood isolate of Staphylococcus aureus is oxacillin susceptible and beta-lactamase (penicillinase) positive. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is MSSA; penicillin G is inactivated, but nafcillin or oxacillin remain appropriate
options.rationale: Correct. Penicillinase hydrolyses penicillin G; oxacillin susceptibility classifies the isolate as MSSA, for which antistaphylococcal penicillins are standard therapy.

options.text: It is MRSA; avoid all beta-lactams
options.rationale: Incorrect. MRSA depends on PBP2a (mecA), usually shown by oxacillin resistance, not by penicillinase.

options.text: Penicillin G is the drug of choice
The beta-lactamase result has no therapeutic meaning
options.rationale: Incorrect. It rules out penicillin G for this isolate.

questions.stem: Under the 2021 IDSA/SHEA focused update, which drug is preferred for an initial episode of Clostridioides difficile infection?

options.rationale: Correct. The 2021 update gives fidaxomicin preferred status over vancomycin; oral vancomycin remains an endorsed option.
Incorrect. IDSA/SHEA removed metronidazole as a preferred option for mild CDI in 2017; some other guidelines keep it for low-risk mild disease or when fidaxomicin and vancomycin are limited.
Incorrect. Clindamycin carried the highest CDI risk of any antibiotic class in a community-associated CDI meta-analysis.
Incorrect. Fluoroquinolones also raise CDI risk and are not CDI treatments.

questions.stem: An adult admitted with acute respiratory illness, ill for 5 days, has a positive influenza molecular assay. What does the IDSA 2018 guideline support?

options.text: Start a neuraminidase inhibitor as soon as possible; CDC also advises Droplet Precautions
options.rationale: Correct. Hospitalized patients are treated as soon as possible regardless of illness duration, and CDC recommends Droplet Precautions.

options.text: Withhold antivirals because symptoms began more than 2 days ago
options.rationale: Incorrect. For hospitalized patients, treatment is recommended regardless of illness duration before admission.

options.text: Wait for viral culture before treating
options.rationale: Incorrect. Viral culture is not recommended for initial diagnosis, and empiric treatment should not wait for results.

options.text: Confirm with a rapid antigen test before treating
options.rationale: Incorrect. Rapid antigen tests are less sensitive and are not recommended in hospitalized patients when molecular assays are available.

claims.text: Penicillinase hydrolyses penicillin (benzylpenicillin); methicillin resistance is PBP2a (mecA); oxacillin-susceptible isolates are classified MSSA on susceptibility testing, with rare mecA-positive OS-MRSA; nafcillin/oxacillin standard, cefazolin common alternative.
Penicillinase is inducible; nitrocefin can miss it; zone-edge test recommended alongside.

CDI drugs: fidaxomicin preferred by IDSA/SHEA (2021), oral vancomycin endorsed, metronidazole not preferred by IDSA/SHEA since 2017; other guidelines allow it for low-risk mild disease or when the others are limited; fulminant regimens add IV metronidazole.
claims.note: The 2021 IDSA/SHEA update itself was not read; its content is taken from Bainum 2023.

claims.text: Clindamycin carries the highest CDI risk among antibiotic classes (OR about 17); fluoroquinolones about 5.5.
Metronidazole first-line for Giardia (cure about 80–95%); tinidazole single-day alternative; refractory cases reported rising in low-prevalence settings, especially travellers returning from Asia.
Hospitalized influenza: molecular testing; no RIDT unless no molecular assay; no culture for initial diagnosis; neuraminidase inhibitor ASAP regardless of illness duration; do not wait for results.
Droplet Precautions for 7 days or until 24 h after symptom resolution, whichever is longer; private room; facemask.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 27 lists oral vancomycin as first-line with fidaxomicin in brackets. Bainum 2023 reports that the 2021 IDSA/SHEA focused update gives fidaxomicin preferred status over vancomycin; vancomycin remains endorsed. The lesson teaches fidaxomicin as preferred (register flag rv-cdi-fidaxomicin-preferred).

Hit 23 equates beta-lactamase-positive, oxacillin-susceptible S. aureus with MSSA. That is the phenotypic classification, but Brahma 2019 and Andrade-Figueiredo 2016 report oxacillin-susceptible mecA-positive isolates (OS-MRSA) that susceptibility testing alone would call MSSA. The lesson teaches the classification with this caveat (register flag rv-ch66-oxa-s-os-mrsa; see also rv-oxacillin-s-mecc for mecC).

Hit 29 (metronidazole first-line for Giardia) is supported by Lalle 2018, but the same review reports rising nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis, especially in infections acquired in Asia, and tinidazole is a single-dose alternative. Not raised as a register flag.

The influenza testing/treatment rules (IDSA) and Droplet Precautions (CDC) are US guidance; Philippine (DOH) infection-control and treatment guidance is not covered. MTLE candidates should check local rules.

Uyeki 2019 and the CDC page were read through a page-fetch tool returning quoted passages, not as downloaded full text; Brown 2013 and Andrade-Figueiredo 2016 were read as abstracts only; the 2021 IDSA/SHEA CDI update was not read directly (its content is taken from Bainum 2023).

morphology.note: No micrographs; results and mechanisms shown as cards.

verification.notes: All 7 factual claims checked against open sources (Uyeki 2019 and the CDC page via a page-fetch tool; Brown 2013 and Andrade-Figueiredo 2016 as abstracts). Independently re-checked by a second fact-checking pass. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
